title: Reverse Linked List
description: Given the head of a singly linked list, reverse the list, and return the reversed list.

examples.explanation: 1->2 becomes 2->1.
An empty list reverses to itself.

hints: You need to flip each node's next pointer.
Keep track of the previous node as you walk the list.
After the loop, the previous node is the new head.

title: Middle of the Linked List
description: Given the head of a singly linked list, return the middle node of the linked list. If there are two middle nodes, return the second middle node.

examples.explanation: The middle node holds 3, so the returned list is 3->4->5.
With two middle nodes, return the second one (4).

hints: A single pass is enough if you use two pointers.
Move one pointer twice as fast as the other.
When the fast pointer reaches the end, the slow pointer sits on the middle.

title: Merge Two Sorted Lists
description: You are given the heads of two sorted linked lists list1 and list2. Merge the two lists into one sorted list. The list should be made by splicing together the nodes of the first two lists. Return the head of the merged linked list.

examples.explanation: Merge picks the smaller current head at each step.
Merging two empty lists gives an empty list.
The non-empty list is the whole merge.

constraints: 0 <= number of nodes in each list <= 50
Both list1 and list2 are sorted in non-decreasing order.
hints: A dummy head node removes special-casing for the first element.
Repeatedly attach the smaller of the two current heads.
When one list runs out, attach the rest of the other list.

title: Linked List Cycle
description:
Given the head of a linked list, determine if the linked list has a cycle in it. There is a cycle in a linked list if there is some node in the list that can be reached again by continuously following the next pointer.

Harness input convention: the single input line is an integer array whose LAST element is pos -- the 0-based index of the node that the tail's next pointer connects to, or -1 for no cycle. The list itself is built from all preceding elements. For example, the input [3, 2, 0, -4, 1] encodes the list 3 -> 2 -> 0 -> -4 with the tail linking back to the node at index 1 (value 2), so the answer is true. The input [1, 2, -1] encodes 1 -> 2 with no cycle, so the answer is false. An input with fewer than two elements (e.g. [] or [-1]) encodes an empty list with no cycle.

examples.explanation: The tail (-4) links back to the node at index 1 (value 2), forming a cycle.
The tail (2) links back to the head (1), forming a cycle.
The single node's next is null, so there is no cycle.

constraints: pos is -1 or a valid index of the list.
hints: Walk the list while remembering visited nodes -- a repeat means a cycle.
Two pointers at different speeds use O(1) space: if they ever meet, there is a cycle.
If the fast pointer hits null, the list ends and there is no cycle.

title: Palindrome Linked List
description: Given the head of a singly linked list, return true if it is a palindrome or false otherwise.

examples.explanation: 1->2->2->1 reads the same forwards and backwards.
1->2 reversed is 2->1, which differs.

hints: A palindrome reads the same forwards and backwards.
Find the middle, then reverse the second half in place.
Compare the two halves node by node; an odd middle node needs no partner.

title: Remove Duplicates from Sorted List
description: Given the head of a sorted linked list, delete all duplicates such that each element appears only once. Return the linked list sorted as well.

examples.explanation: The duplicate 1 is removed.
The duplicates of 1 and 3 are removed.

constraints: The list is sorted in non-decreasing order.
hints: Because the list is sorted, equal values are always adjacent.
Compare each node with its next node as you walk.
When they match, bypass the next node instead of advancing.

title: Remove Linked List Elements
description: Given the head of a linked list and an integer val, remove all the nodes of the linked list that have Node.val == val, and return the new head.

examples.explanation: Both nodes with value 6 are removed.
Nothing to remove from an empty list.
Every node is removed, leaving an empty list.

hints: Nodes to delete can include the head -- plan for that.
A dummy node before the head unifies the removal logic.
Only advance past a node when you keep it.

title: Convert Binary Number in a Linked List to Integer
description: Given head which is a reference node to a singly-linked list. The value of each node in the linked list is either 0 or 1. The linked list holds the binary representation of a number. Return the decimal value of the number in the linked list. The most significant bit is at the head of the linked list.

examples.explanation: Binary 101 equals 5 in decimal.
Binary 0 equals 0.

hints: Read the bits from head (most significant) to tail.
Each step: double the running value, then add the current bit.
That is: result = result * 2 + node.val.

title: Add Two Numbers
description: You are given two non-empty linked lists representing two non-negative integers. The digits are stored in reverse order, and each of their nodes contains a single digit. Add the two numbers and return the sum as a linked list. You may assume the two numbers do not contain any leading zeros, except the number 0 itself.

examples.explanation: 342 + 465 = 807, stored reversed as 7->0->8.

constraints: 1 <= number of nodes in each list <= 100
Each list represents a number with no leading zeros.
hints: Add digit by digit like column addition, tracking a carry.
The lists may have different lengths -- treat missing digits as 0.
Do not forget: a final carry can add one more node.

title: Remove Nth Node From End of List
description: Given the head of a linked list, remove the nth node from the end of the list and return its head.

examples.explanation: The 2nd node from the end (4) is removed.
Removing the only node leaves an empty list.
The last node (2) is removed.

hints: The nth node from the end is the (length - n + 1)th node from the start.
Two pointers n apart let you find it in one pass.
A dummy head handles the case where the head itself is removed.

title: Swap Nodes in Pairs
description: Given a linked list, swap every two adjacent nodes and return its head. You must solve the problem without modifying the values in the list's nodes (i.e., only nodes themselves may be changed).

examples.explanation: Pairs (1,2) and (3,4) are each swapped.
An empty list has no pairs.
A single node has no partner and stays put.

hints: Swap the nodes themselves, not their values.
Handle each pair through a pointer to the node before the pair.
After swapping, the old first node of the pair becomes the anchor for the next pair.

title: Reorder List
description: You are given the head of a singly linked list. Reorder the list in place so that it becomes L0 -> Ln -> L1 -> Ln-1 -> L2 -> Ln-2 -> ... . You may not modify the values in the list's nodes; only the nodes themselves may be changed. The method returns void -- reorder the given list in place. (The harness only checks that the method runs without error, so the expected output is empty for every test.)

examples.explanation: Reordered in place as 1->4->2->3 (the method itself returns void).
Reordered in place as 1->5->2->4->3 (the method itself returns void).

hints: Break it into steps: find the middle, reverse the second half, then merge.
Merging weaves one node from the front half and one from the reversed back half.
Stop the merge when the back half runs out.

title: Odd Even Linked List
description: Given the head of a singly linked list, group all the nodes with odd indices together followed by the nodes with even indices, and return the reordered list. The first node is considered odd, the second node is even, and so on. The relative order inside both the even and odd groups must stay as it was in the input. Solve it in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

examples.explanation: Odd positions (1,3,5) come first, then even positions (2,4).
Odd positions (2,3,6,7) come first, then even positions (1,5,4).

hints: Positions (1st, 2nd, ...) decide the groups, not the values.
Maintain separate odd and even chains as you walk once.
Finally, link the odd chain's tail to the even chain's head.

title: Rotate List
description: Given the head of a linked list, rotate the list to the right by k places.

examples.explanation: The last 2 nodes move to the front.
k = 4 is equivalent to k = 1 for a 3-node list.

hints: Rotating right by k equals rotating by k mod length.
Link the tail to the head to form a ring, then cut it at the new tail.
The new tail is length - (k mod length) steps from the old head.

title: Partition List
description: Given the head of a linked list and a value x, partition it such that all nodes less than x come before nodes greater than or equal to x. Preserve the original relative order of the nodes in each of the two partitions.

examples.explanation: Nodes < 3 (1,2,2) come first, then nodes >= 3 (4,3,5), each in original order.
1 < 2 moves before 2.

hints: Two passes or one pass with two lists both work -- keep relative order.
Build a 'before x' list and an 'after x' list, appending to each tail.
Join them and set the final tail's next to null.

title: Sort List
description: Given the head of a linked list, return the list sorted in ascending order.

examples.explanation: The list sorted in ascending order.
The list sorted in ascending order.
An empty list is already sorted.

hints: Merge sort suits linked lists: no random access needed.
Split with slow/fast pointers, sort each half, then merge.
Merging two sorted lists takes O(n) time and O(1) space.

title: Reverse Nodes in k-Group
description: Given the head of a linked list, reverse the nodes of the list k at a time, and return the modified list. k is a positive integer and is less than or equal to the length of the linked list. If the number of nodes is not a multiple of k, the left-out nodes at the end stay as-is. You may not alter the values in the list's nodes; only the nodes themselves may be changed.

examples.explanation: Groups (1,2) and (3,4) are reversed; the leftover 5 stays.
Group (1,2,3) is reversed; (4,5) is too short and stays.

hints: Only reverse a group when k full nodes remain.
Reverse one group of k, link it, then continue from the next group.
Track the node before each group so the reversed group can be reattached.

title: LRU Cache
description:
Design a data structure that follows the constraints of a Least Recently Used (LRU) cache, exposed through a single method:

int[] lruCache(int capacity, String[] ops, String[] args)

The method receives a sequence of operations to run on a fresh cache with the given capacity, and returns the results of all "get" operations in order, as an int array.

Operation format: ops[i] is either "put" or "get". args[i] carries that operation's arguments as a string: for "get" it is just the key (e.g. "1"); for "put" it is "key,value" (e.g. "1,10"). Keys and values are integers.

Semantics: get(key) returns the key's value, or -1 if the key is absent. Every get or put marks the key as most recently used. put(key, value) inserts a new key or updates an existing one; if the cache already holds capacity keys, evict the least recently used key before inserting.

Example: capacity = 2, ops = ["put","put","get","put","get","get"], args = ["1,1","2,2","1","3,3","2","3"]. put(1,1), put(2,2), get(1) -> 1, put(3,3) evicts key 2, get(2) -> -1, get(3) -> 3. Return [1, -1, 3].

examples.explanation: get(1)=1; put(3,3) evicts key 2; get(2)=-1; get(3)=3.
get(5) returns the stored value 50.

hints: You need O(1) lookup and O(1) recency updates.
Pair a hash map (key -> node) with a doubly linked list (recency order).
Every get/put moves the key to the most-recent end; evict from the least-recent end.

title: Remove Zero Sum Consecutive Nodes from Linked List
description: Given the head of a linked list, repeatedly delete every consecutive sequence of nodes that sums to 0, until no such sequence remains. Return the head of the final linked list.

examples.explanation: The consecutive sequence 3,-3 sums to 0 and is removed.
Removing 3,-3 gives 1,2,-2; then 2,-2 sums to 0 and is removed, leaving 1.
The whole list sums to 0 and is removed.

hints: Prefix sums turn 'subarray sums to 0' into 'a prefix sum repeats'.
Map each prefix sum to its LAST occurrence in one pass.
In a second pass, jump each node directly past its last repeated prefix sum.

title: LFU Cache
description:
Design a data structure that follows the constraints of a Least Frequently Used (LFU) cache, exposed through a single method:

int[] lfuCache(int capacity, String[] ops, String[] args)

The method receives a sequence of operations to run on a fresh cache with the given capacity, and returns the results of all "get" operations in order, as an int array. The ops/args format is the same as the LRU cache problem: ops[i] is "put" or "get"; args[i] is the key for "get" (e.g. "1") or "key,value" for "put" (e.g. "1,10").

Semantics: get(key) returns the key's value, or -1 if the key is absent. Every get, and every put on an existing key, increments that key's use-frequency. put(key, value) inserts or updates; a newly inserted key starts with frequency 1. If the cache is full, evict the key with the smallest frequency, breaking ties by least recently used. (A capacity of 0 means nothing is ever stored: every get returns -1.)

Example: capacity = 2, ops = ["put","put","get","put","get","get","get"], args = ["1,1","2,2","1","3,3","2","3","1"]. put(1,1) [freq 1], put(2,2) [freq 1], get(1) -> 1 [freq 2], put(3,3) evicts key 2 (frequency 1 < 2), get(2) -> -1, get(3) -> 3 [freq 2], get(1) -> 1. Return [1, -1, 3, 1].

examples.explanation: get(1)=1; put(3,3) evicts key 2 (lower frequency); get(2)=-1; get(3)=3; get(1)=1.
put(3,3) evicts key 1 (frequency tie broken by recency); get(2)=2.

hints: Track each key's frequency and recency.
Group keys by frequency so the minimum is always at hand.
Both get and put-on-existing-key bump the frequency and refresh recency.
